Let $s_t(n)$ be the $t$-smooth component of $n$ - that is, the product of all primes $p$ (with multiplicity) dividing $n$ such that $p<t$. Let $f(n,t)$ count the number of distinct possible values for $s_t(m)$ for $m\in [n+1,n+t]$. Is it true that\[f(n,t)\gg t\](uniformly, for all $t$ and $n$)?

 Here is a guess to Erdos #461: the bound $f(n,t)\ge t/2$ cannot hold asymptotically.
Let $s_t(m)$ denote the $t$-smooth component of $m$, and let
$$
f(n,t)=|\{s_t(n+1),\ldots,s_t(n+t)\}|.
$$
For $y<t$,
$$
f(n,t)\le y+|\{1\le i\le t:s_t(n+i)>y\}|,
$$
since at most $y$ distinct values can lie in $[1,y]$. Put
$$
P_t=\prod_{p<t}p,\qquad Q=P_t\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,y).
$$
For each $u\le y$, $u$ is automatically $t$-smooth, and
$$
s_t(m)=u
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
m=ur,\ (r,P_t)=1.
$$
Thus, over one period modulo $Q$,
$$
\frac1Q|\{m\bmod Q:s_t(m)=u\}| = 
\frac1u\prod_{p<t}\left(1-\frac1p\right).
$$
Averaging the truncation inequality over $n\bmod Q$, and using that $n\mapsto n+i$ permutes residue classes modulo $Q$, gives
$$
\inf_n f(n,t)
\le
y+t\left(1-\prod_{p<t}\left(1-\frac1p\right)H_y\right),
$$
where $H_y=\sum_{u\le y}1/u$. Taking
$$
y\sim \frac{e^{-\gamma}t}{\log t}
$$
and using Mertens’ theorem yields
$$
\inf_n f(n,t)\le (1-e^{-\gamma}+o(1))t.
$$
Hence no universal lower bound $f(n,t)\ge ct)$ can hold with $c>1-e^{-\gamma}\approx0.4385$; in particular, the $c=1/2$ strengthening is false. This does not settle Problem #461, which only asks whether $f(n,t)\gg t$.
Proof assisted by GPT 5.5 Pro and Claude Fable. Would be thankful for any proposals to amend.

 Thank you for your kind observations! I should clarify that the \(t/2\) threshold was not meant to be attributed to Erdős--Graham, and does not settle the original question \(f(n,t)\gg t\). 
It came from Woett's idea from the comment below: if the proposed bipartite graph always had a matching covering \(\{1,\ldots,\lfloor t/2\rfloor\}\), then one would get \(f(n,t)\ge\lfloor t/2\rfloor\). Since Woett already showed that matching statement is false, I treated \(t/2\) only as a temporary strengthened guess suggested by the heuristic.
The averaging argument only rules out that strengthened \(1/2\) guess, and more generally any lower bound \(f(n,t)\ge c t\) with \(c>1-e^{-\gamma}\). 
I also agree this is likely a standard first-moment/smooth-part calculation without novelty. The local density\[
\Pr(s_t(m)=u)=\frac1u\prod_{p<t}(1-1/p)
\]is the usual count for integers with a prescribed \(t\)-smooth part / largest smooth divisor, followed by Mertens' theorem. This reply is checked against GPT 5.5 pro and opus 4.8. Many thanks!

 A further update to my earlier upper-bound observation. Let
$$
F(t):=\min_n f(n,t).
$$
Then
$$
\boxed{
F(t)\le (1-\log 2)t+
O\!\left(\frac{t\log\log t}{\log t}\right)
}
$$
and hence
$$
\limsup_{t\to\infty}\frac{F(t)}t
\le 1-\log2
=0.306852819440\ldots .
$$
Here is the argument. Put
$$
L=\lceil\log_2t\rceil,\qquad
K=\lfloor t/L\rfloor,\qquad
X=Kt,
$$
and partition \((X,2X]\) into its \(K\) consecutive intervals of length \(t\).
For large \(t\), \(2X<t^2\) and \(2K<t\). Hence if \(m\in(X,2X]\) is not \(t\)-smooth, with the strict convention that only primes \(p<t\) belong to \(s_t(m)\), then \(m\) has exactly one prime factor \(p\ge t\), occurring to exponent one. Writing
$$
m=pa,
$$
we have
$$
a\le\frac{2X}{t}=2K<t.
$$
Thus every prime factor of \(a\) is \(<t\), and therefore
$$
s_t(m)=a\le2K.
$$
Consequently all nonsmooth integers in any one window contribute at most \(2K=O(t/\log t)\) distinct labels.
Every genuinely \(t\)-smooth integer \(m\) instead has \(s_t(m)=m\), so these labels are mutually distinct and cannot overlap the nonsmooth labels, since \(m>X>2K\).
Let \(S_j\) denote the number of genuinely \(t\)-smooth integers in the \(j\)-th window. Then
$$
f(n_j,t)\le S_j+2K.
$$
For \(Z<t^2\),
$$
\Psi_{<t}(Z)
=
Z-\sum_{\substack{t\le p\le Z\\p\ {\rm prime}}}
\left\lfloor\frac Zp\right\rfloor,
$$
because an integer below \(t^2\) cannot be divisible by two distinct primes \(\ge t\), nor by the square of one.
Mertens' theorem gives
$$
\sum_{t\le p\le Z}\frac1p
=
\log\frac{\log Z}{\log t}
+O\!\left(\frac1{\log t}\right).
$$
Now, with
$$
\beta=\frac{\log L}{\log t},
$$
we have
$$
\frac{\log X}{\log t}
=
2-\beta+o(1/\log t),
\qquad
\beta=O\!\left(\frac{\log\log t}{\log t}\right),
$$
and similarly for \(2X\). Hence
$$
\log\frac{\log Z}{\log t}
=
\log2+
O\!\left(\frac{\log\log t}{\log t}\right)
$$
for \(Z=X,2X\). The floor errors contribute only \(O(Z/\log Z)\), so
$$
\Psi_{<t}(Z)
=
(1-\log2)Z+
O\!\left(\frac{Z\log\log t}{\log t}\right).
$$
Averaging over the \(K\) windows therefore gives one \(j\) such that
$$
S_j\le
(1-\log2)t+
O\!\left(\frac{t\log\log t}{\log t}\right).
$$
Since \(2K=O(t/\log t)\), the claimed bound follows.
Equivalently, the leading constant is the classical Dickman value
$$
\rho(2)=1-\log2.
$$
This is only an upper construction and does not settle Erdős #461, which asks whether \(f(n,t)\gg t\) uniformly.

 This may be trivial and well-known (but I have reached few times), as a range-restricted improvement for the Erdos-Graham bound. It is uniform for n\(\le t^K\)
, but not uniform in arbitrary n. It beats Erdős–Graham by a factor loglogt, but (i) only for shifts of polynomial height; and (ii) says nothing new for n growing faster than every fixed power of t.
Let \(K\ge 1\). I believe that, uniformly for \(0\le n\le t^K\),\[
f(n,t)\gg_K \frac{t\log\log t}{\log t}.
\]This is weaker than the known restricted-height linear result in the
smaller range \(n+t\le t^{43/30-\varepsilon}\), but applies to every
fixed polynomial height.
Let\[
L_t^-=\prod_{\substack{p<t\\ p^{a_p}\le t<p^{a_p+1}}}p^{a_p},
\qquad
\widehat u_i=\gcd(n+i,L_t^-).
\]Counting multiples of each prime power gives\[
\sum_{i=1}^t\log \widehat u_i
\ge
\sum_{\substack{p^a\le t\\p<t}}
\Big\lfloor\frac{t}{p^a}\Big\rfloor\log p
=
\log(t!)-O(\log t)
=
t\log t-O(t).
\tag{1}
\]Write \(u_i=s_t(n+i)\), let \(S\) be the singleton rows, and put\[
s=|S|,\qquad R=t-s,\qquad F=f(n,t),\qquad k=F-s.
\]If a label \(u\) occurs \(m_u\ge2\) times, fibre spacing gives
\(2u(m_u-1)\le t-1\), hence \(u\le t/m_u\). Therefore, by concavity,\[
\sum_{\substack{u\\m_u\ge2}}m_u\log\widehat u
\le
\sum_{\substack{u\\m_u\ge2}}m_u\log\frac{t}{m_u}
\le
R\log\frac{tk}{R}.
\tag{2}
\]For \(i\in S\),\[
\widehat u_i\le n+i\le 2t^K,
\]so\[
\sum_{i\in S}\log\widehat u_i\le (K+1)s\log t.
\tag{3}
\]Combining (1)--(3),\[
t\log t-O(t)
\le
R\log\frac{tk}{R}+(K+1)s\log t.
\]Writing \(\alpha=F/t<1/2\), and using\[
R\ge(1-\alpha)t,\qquad k\le\alpha t,\qquad s\le\alpha t,
\]we obtain\[
(1-\alpha)\log\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}
\le
K\alpha\log t+O(1).
\]Hence\[
\alpha\gg_K\frac{\log\log t}{\log t},
\]as claimed.
The limitation is transparent: the argument controls singleton mass by
\(\log(n+t)\). For polynomial \(n\), no small collection of singleton
rows can absorb the total \(t\log t\) capped-mass budget. For arbitrary
height, however, a few rows may carry exceptionally large smooth parts,
so this estimate degenerates and does not address the unrestricted
problem.
This observation was developed with assistance from GPT-5.6 and Claude
Opus; references or corrections would be very welcome.

 After many tries for a natural entropy approach to Problem 461, it seems any akibg sycg lines would be a no-go. A proof cannot proceed by proving a uniform entropy-deficit bound of size
𝑂⁡(𝑡), or even 𝑂⁡(𝑡⁢log⁡log⁡𝑡).
For a ruler datum\[
\beta=(\beta_p \bmod p^{K_p})_{p<t},\qquad
K_p=\min\{k:p^k>t\},
\]write\[
D(\beta)=\{1\le x\le t:\exists p<t,\ x+\beta_p\equiv0\pmod {p^{K_p}}\},
\]and for \(x\notin D(\beta)\),\[
L_\beta(x)=\prod_{p<t}p^{v_p(x+\beta_p)}.
\]Deep positions may be treated as singleton artificial labels. Let
\(m_\alpha\) be the multiplicity of the label \(\alpha\), so that\[
F_t(\beta)=\#\{\alpha:m_\alpha>0\}.
\]A tempting route is to use entropy. If \(X\) is uniform on
\(\{1,\ldots,t\}\), and \(A\) is its label, then\[
H(A)
=
\log t-\frac1t\sum_\alpha m_\alpha\log m_\alpha.
\]Since \(H(A)\le \log F_t(\beta)\), one obtains\[
F_t(\beta)
\ge
t\exp\!\left(
-\frac1t\sum_\alpha m_\alpha\log m_\alpha
\right).
\]Thus a uniform estimate\[
\sum_\alpha m_\alpha\log m_\alpha=O(t)
\]would imply the desired linear lower bound.
However this entropy-deficit estimate is false, even for genuine all-prime
ruler data.
Choose the residues \(\beta_p\bmod p^{K_p}\) independently and uniformly.
Put\[
V_t=\prod_{p<t}\left(1-\frac1p\right)
\sim \frac{e^{-\gamma}}{\log t}.
\]For any admissible ordinary label \(u\), and fixed \(x\),\[
\mathbb P(L_\beta(x)=u)=\frac{V_t}{u}.
\]Therefore\[
\mathbb E m_u=\frac{tV_t}{u}.
\]Let \(N_t=tV_t\). For \(1\le u\le N_t\), \(u\) is admissible for all
large \(t\). Since \(z\log z\) is convex,\[
\mathbb E[m_u\log m_u]
\ge
\frac{N_t}{u}\log\frac{N_t}{u}.
\]Hence\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E\sum_\alpha m_\alpha\log m_\alpha
&\ge
N_t\sum_{u\le N_t}\frac{\log(N_t/u)}u \\
&=
\left(\frac12+o(1)\right)N_t(\log N_t)^2 \\
&=
\left(\frac{e^{-\gamma}}2+o(1)\right)t\log t.
\end{aligned}
\]Consequently, for arbitrarily large \(t\), there are genuine ruler data
with\[
\sum_\alpha m_\alpha\log m_\alpha
\ge
\left(\frac{e^{-\gamma}}2+o(1)\right)t\log t.
\]Since trivially\[
\sum_\alpha m_\alpha\log m_\alpha\le t\log t,
\]the worst-case entropy deficit is \(\Theta(t\log t)\).
So the Shannon-entropy sufficient condition is much too strong. 
However a more support-sensitive invariant which tolerates this Zipf-type random-ruler obstruction while still
forcing \(F_t(\beta)\gg t\).
Write up is assisted by GPT 5.6.

 An idea I had that doesn't quite work as stated: for a given $n$ and $t$, consider the bipartite graph with left vertex set $\mathcal{L} := \{1, 2, \ldots, \lfloor t/2 \rfloor\}$, right vertex set $\mathcal{R} := \{s_t(n+1), \ldots, s_t(n+t)\}$, and where we draw an edge between $i \in \mathcal{L}$ and $s_t(m) \in \mathcal{R}$ if $i$ divides $s_t(m)$ (which in this case is equivalent to $i$ dividing $m$, as $i < t$). If there is a matching that covers all vertices of the left set, then we would be done.
However, such a matching unfortunately does not always exist. ChatGPT managed to find the counterexample $n = 1407302$, $t = 38$. Here, with $$D := \{13, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19\} \subset \mathcal{L},$$the neighbourhood of $D$ in $\mathcal{R}$ only contains the $5 < |D|$ integers $s_t(m)$ with $$m - n \in \{9, 10, 13, 26, 28\}.$$
